subject.title: Dreams
subject.author: Arthur Symons
subject.text:
I
To dream of love, and, waking, to remember you:
As though, being dead, one dreamed of heaven, and woke
      in hell.
At night my lovely dreams forget the old farewell:
Ah! wake not by his side, lest you remember too!


                                  II
I set all Rome between us: with what joy I set
The wonder of the world against my world's delight!
Rome, that hast conquered worlds, with intellectual might
Capture my heart, and teach my memory to forget!

title: He Set Rome Between Himself and a Memory. It Didn't Hold.
standfirst: Arthur Symons spent his career trusting that distance, intellect and the right foreign city could argue a person out of grief — in an earlier book about a lover he never named, in his own travel writing, and in this stray 1918 poem, printed a decade after the one trip that proved the theory wrong.

sections.heading: A Poem Built From Two Different Kinds of Trying
sections.body:
"Dreams" splits cleanly down the middle, and its two halves don't agree with each other. The first describes something the speaker can't control:

> To dream of love, and, waking, to remember you:
> As though, being dead, one dreamed of heaven, and woke
>       in hell.
> At night my lovely dreams forget the old farewell:
> Ah! wake not by his side, lest you remember too!

Sleep is treacherous here precisely because it is honest. It forgets "the old farewell" — the agreed ending, the breakup — and hands the love back whole, so that waking into the real arrangement again feels like a fall from heaven straight into hell. The fear even runs outward: the speaker worries that the woman he's addressing, who now sleeps by another man's side, might be caught by the same undefended memory on some ordinary morning of her own.

The second half answers with a plan instead of a confession:

> I set all Rome between us: with what joy I set
> The wonder of the world against my world's delight!
> Rome, that hast conquered worlds, with intellectual might
> Capture my heart, and teach my memory to forget!

This is a different register entirely — not something that happened to him, but something he arranged, and is still half-bragging about ("with what joy I set"). Read together, the two halves turn the poem into a small, quiet progress report on a failed strategy: a man who built a defence against grief, and a dream life that keeps finding the gap in it.

sections.heading: A Line Too Long to Be Native English
sections.body: Say the lines out loud and they run long — longer than the ten-syllable pentameter that carries most English lyric, closer to the twelve-syllable alexandrine that is the working line of French verse instead. "To dream of love, and, waking, to remember you" takes twelve syllables to do what an English love poem usually does in ten; "I set all Rome between us: with what joy I set" does the same. That isn't an idle tic. Symons spent the 1890s translating, defending and all but worshipping French poetry, Paul Verlaine above all — by his own biographers' account he wrote more about Verlaine than about any other writer, translated a large share of his work, and helped organise an [English lecture tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Symons) for him. When Symons published *London Nights* in 1895, he dedicated it to Verlaine outright, in French: "en témoignage d'amitié et d'admiration" — as a token of friendship and admiration. A man who had built that much of his name on importing French rhythm into English verse reaching, late and almost without noticing, for the French line's extra two syllables reads less like a slip than like handwriting.

sections.heading: The Woman He Spent a Whole Book Not Naming
sections.body:
The unnamed "you" in "Dreams" is not an isolated reticence. Around 1893 Symons began a long relationship with a lover he never identified to the outside world, referring to her only as "Lydia," and built an entire book, *[Amoris Victima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Symons)* (1897) — Latin for "victim of love" — around the affair without ever supplying her name. The record has its own tangle here: Symons's mother was also called Lydia, and died in March 1896, in the middle of the years the affair is said to have run, though nothing in the sources connects the two women beyond the coincidence of the name.

What matters for "Dreams" is the habit, not the particular woman. Discretion, for Symons, wasn't a lapse in an otherwise confessional poetry — it was closer to a method. A poem that will not name the person it's grieving, written by a man who had already spent a whole collection not naming someone else, reads less like shyness than like a writer returning to a technique that had already served him once.

sections.heading: A City He Had Actually Been To
sections.body:
"Rome" in the second stanza isn't a rhyme-driven abstraction, a grand noun reached for because the line needed one. Symons wrote whole books out of Italy: *Cities* (1903) gathered what one contemporary review called his "word-pictures" of Rome, Venice, Naples and Seville, and a later scholarly collection on his work devotes an entire chapter to what it calls "[Symons on Italy and the Metamorphoses of Aesthetic Travel Writing](https://www.mhra.org.uk/publications/sicl-44)." He went back to the country repeatedly across more than a decade, turning what he saw there into essays as a matter of professional habit.

That makes the poem's central move more interesting than it first looks. The plan in "Dreams" isn't just travel as distraction — it's a specific theory about scale: that something old enough and vast enough, a city that "hast conquered worlds," might out-argue one person's grief through sheer "intellectual might." It's the kind of claim a man makes about a place he has actually stood in and measured himself against, repeatedly, not one he's borrowing for effect.

sections.heading: The Trip That Argued Back
sections.body:
In 1908, a decade after *Amoris Victima*, Symons and his wife Rhoda — he had married Rhoda Bowser in 1901 — took a tour of Europe funded partly on borrowed money, after word reached him that an Italian translation of his play *Tristan and Iseult* was to be staged there. In Venice he grew overstimulated and feverish, left Rhoda behind, and moved restlessly between hotels. He then vanished into the countryside for two days, exhausted and, in [Wikipedia's phrase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Symons), showing "symptoms of madness," before being found and arrested — by two Italian soldiers near Ferrara, that account says, though an [EBSCO summary of the episode](https://ebsco.com/research-starters/history/arthur-symons) instead places the arrest in Bologna, after days of Symons "acting irrationally" in the streets. The two accounts don't agree on the town. They agree on everything after it: an Italian asylum, a slow transfer into Rhoda's custody, an English hospital at Crowborough in Sussex from which he tried to escape, and a move afterward to a cheaper institution with fewer facilities. He wrote about the whole collapse himself, decades later, in *Confessions: A Study in Pathology* (1930).

There is one odd piece of hindsight sitting in the record: a 2018 academic collection on Symons includes a chapter simply titled "['They Keep Mad People There': Symons and Venice](https://www.mhra.org.uk/publications/sicl-44)." Whatever that essay actually argues, the title alone is hard to read now as anything but a diagnosis arriving ten years too late to help him.

sections.heading: A Decadent's Couplets Arrive in a Magazine Already Moving Past Him
sections.body:
"Dreams" ran in *Poetry* magazine in August 1918 — volume 12, number 5, edited by Harriet Monroe — on pages 252 and 253, with a second Symons poem, "To a Grey Dress," on the [facing page of the same issue](https://modjourn.org/issue/bdr461880/). The rest of that issue belongs to a different literary moment entirely: poems about ambulances and war-sketched woods, Amy Lowell, a translation from Konstantin Balmont, and, deep in the back pages, a piece of correspondence credited to "Emanuel Morgan" — the invented poet Witter Bynner had used two years earlier, alongside Arthur Davison Ficke writing as "Anne Knish," to run the [Spectra hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectra_%28poetry_collection%29), a deadpan fake movement built to mock Imagism that fooled reviewers for the better part of two years before Bynner admitted the joke, in public, that same year.

Symons was the one person in that table of contents who had actually done, in earnest and two decades earlier, something close to what *Spectra* existed to ridicule — importing a self-consciously advanced continental sensibility into English verse and being taken entirely seriously for it. His own contribution is a pair of rhymed, regular, old-fashioned stanzas about failing to forget a woman. Wikipedia's flat verdict on his last decades is that he "published little new work for more than twenty years" after 1908; "Dreams" is one of the small exceptions. Ten years after his own trip to Italy ended in an asylum ward, he was still publishing a poem that trusted Rome's "intellectual might" to out-argue a memory — a theory his own life, in the one country he had actually gone to test it in, had already watched fail.
